title: Master Class | Veresov / Benoni | Chess Speedrun | Grandmaster Naroditsky

moves.spoken: Finally we get White — and we're going to play the mainline, d4 and c4, grabbing the big classical center.
This is the Nimzo-Indian territory, and there are three main systems White can choose against it — all reputable, all positionally rich.
The knight to c3 keeps us in the most positionally rich waters.
Black strikes with c5 — he's steering into the Benoni.
This is one of several move orders into the Benoni; Black can also play c5 here and transpose after the knight to c3.
So after c5, the knight to c3, e6, we head into a mainline Benoni with d5.
d5, clamping down and gaining space in the center.
Black plays d6 immediately, which is a bit inaccurate — a little passive; not terrible, but passive.
How should White expand? The typical Benoni move, of course, is e4, building the full pawn center — and comparing move orders is exactly what reveals why d6 was slightly off.
Comparison often yields wisdom about a position you'd otherwise miss. Black develops the bishop to e7.
The bishop to d3 is the right square, anticipating that Black will probably capture on d5 — and even if he doesn't, it's well placed there.
Black plays the knight to d7. There's no need for us to take on c5 — that trade doesn't especially help White.
You could play f4 immediately to grab a pawn, but I don't like that — playing positionally, we simply develop the knight to f3.
Black is cramped, and we're going to squeeze the life out of him. He tries the knight to g4.
No need to go out of our way to stop it — we just castle, because if you calculate a bit further you'll see it resolves in our favor.
Black plays the knight to e5. There's a misconception about pieces in the center — you can't assume a central piece is automatically strong.
The real question is how easily you can chase it, and we'll be able to hit it with f4 — so we take, the knight capturing on e5.
Black recaptures on e5. That knight is good for a couple of moves, but then f4 comes.
Be careful not to automatically drop the bishop to c2 — that would blunder the pawn. The bishop to e2 is precise, and then we hit with a nice f4 with tempo.
Black plays the bishop to f6.
I don't see a reason not to play f4 — let's go.
The bottom line: among the three pawns in front of the king, pushing the f-pawn is the most innocuous, because you're not actually shattering the king's shell.
You still have your g- and h-pawns, and you can always tuck the king over to h1 — so f4 and the knight to g6 is nothing to fear.
Making a move like g4 is infinitely more weakening — that doesn't mean you never play it, but the danger comes when you push all three pawns in front of your king.
So f4 and the knight to g6 leaves a very rich position, fully sound for White.
The bishop to e3 is important, and we've also got interesting ideas with an e5 break brewing.
Black castles.
Now look at the d-file: there's a weak backward pawn on d6. We take, d5 takes e6, opening the file and putting that weakness on trial.
Black recaptures with the bishop on e6 — and now all of White's pieces coordinate beautifully.
f5 — a fork, hitting the bishop and the knight at once.
Black saves the bishop with the retreat to d7.
We take, f takes g6, ripping open the kingside.
Black recaptures on g6.
The queen scoops up the weak pawn, taking on d6.
The rook to d1 is coming. Black plays b6.
We bring the rook to d1, piling onto the d-file.
Black tries the rook to f7 — but we can't let him escape. How should we continue?
e5 is very natural here — crushing him down every file and every avenue.
